question: Which type of diabetes is most commonly linked to Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS)?
explanation: HHS usually occurs in older adults with type 2 diabetes who experience severe dehydration. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h1)

question: How does the onset of HHS usually compare to diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?

options.A: HHS develops much more slowly over weeks
options.B: HHS appears suddenly within a few minutes
options.C: DKA develops over several weeks instead

explanation: While DKA can develop quickly within hours, HHS builds up slowly over days or weeks, causing severe fluid loss before it is noticed. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why do patients with HHS typically not develop severe ketoacidosis?

options.A: Patient diets lack any dietary fat components
options.B: High blood osmolality destroys all body acids
options.C: Residual insulin prevents significant fat breakdown
options.D: The kidneys rapidly excrete all produced ketones

explanation: Even a small amount of remaining insulin stops the breakdown of fats, preventing large amounts of ketones from forming. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h2)

question: What primary process is blocked by the minimal insulin present in HHS?
explanation: Small amounts of insulin are enough to stop the breakdown of fats (lipolysis), which stops the formation of ketones. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h2)

question: What is the single most common trigger for an episode of HHS?
explanation: Infections like pneumonia or urinary tract infections are the most frequent triggers that push a diabetic patient into HHS. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h3)

question: Which medication class taken by an older diabetic patient is most likely to contribute to HHS?
explanation: Diuretics increase fluid loss, which can worsen dehydration and raise blood sugar levels. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h3)

question: Which neurological symptom is most common in advanced HHS?

options.A: Severe sharp pain along the spine
options.D: Sudden loss of hearing in both ears

explanation: High blood concentration pulls water out of brain cells, leading to confusion, extreme tiredness, or coma. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h4)

question: What mechanism causes the extreme fluid loss seen in patients with HHS?

options.A: Direct destruction of kidney tubules by infection
options.B: Excessive sweating due to high body temperature
options.C: Osmotic diuresis driven by high blood glucose
options.D: Failure of the lungs to retain water vapor

explanation: High sugar levels in the kidneys pull large amounts of water into the urine, causing severe dehydration. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h4)

question: What blood glucose level is typically found in a patient with HHS?
explanation: HHS involves very high blood sugar levels, often rising well past 30 mmol/L. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h5)

question: Which laboratory result helps clinicians tell HHS apart from diabetic ketoacidosis?

options.A: Absence of any blood urea nitrogen
options.C: Normal or near-normal arterial blood pH
options.D: Completely clear and normal urine output

explanation: A normal or only slightly low blood pH above 7.30 points away from DKA and toward HHS. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the most urgent treatment priority when managing a patient with HHS?

options.A: Immediate administration of high-dose oral iron
options.B: Complete restriction of all dietary protein

explanation: Giving IV fluids to reverse severe dehydration is the first step to restore circulation and lower blood concentration. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why is fluid therapy often changed from normal saline to half-normal saline as treatment continues?

options.A: To replace intracellular water deficits safely
options.B: To prevent the patient from feeling nauseated
options.C: To quickly raise the body temperature back up
options.D: To stop the kidneys from producing any urine

explanation: Hypotonic fluids provide free water to rehydrate cells that shrank due to high blood concentration. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h6)

question: Why should insulin therapy be delayed until fluid replacement has started in HHS?

options.A: To allow the laboratory time to test kidney function
options.B: Because insulin destroys normal saline inside the vein
options.C: To ensure the patient has eaten a full meal first
options.D: To prevent sudden vascular collapse from rapid fluid shifts

explanation: Giving insulin before fluids causes water to rush from blood vessels into cells, causing blood pressure to drop dangerously. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h7)

question: What electrolyte shift commonly happens when insulin therapy starts during HHS treatment?

options.A: Sodium completely disappears from the bloodstream
options.C: Calcium levels rise to dangerous high values
options.D: Potassium moves into cells, lowering serum levels

explanation: Insulin pushes potassium along with glucose into cells, which can lower blood potassium levels if not monitored. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h7)

question: Which assessment must be done hourly to monitor a patient's recovery from HHS?

options.D: Checking range of motion in the knees

explanation: Frequent neurological checks show whether the brain is recovering as blood osmolality returns to normal. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h8)

question: Which instruction is most important to include in discharge teaching to prevent future episodes of HHS?

options.A: Stop taking all oral medications if feeling tired
options.B: Drink plenty of water and manage early infections
options.C: Avoid eating any carbohydrates for the rest of life
options.D: Check blood pressure only once every six months

explanation: Staying well-hydrated and treating infections early helps prevent the dehydration and stress that trigger HHS. [learn more](BMP216_U2_T4#BMP216_U2_T4_h8)
